seoTitle: Shopify Product Quiz Design: How I Simplified Fuzzball’s Quiz
description: How I redesigned Fuzzball’s Shopify product quiz from a UX review: one input type per screen, fewer steps, a skip option, and a cat progress bar for character.
standfirst: I simplified Fuzzball’s Shopify product quiz by giving every screen one type of answer, cutting the questions that didn’t change the plan and adding a way to skip. Then I gave it back its character with a cat that chases a ball of wool along the progress bar. Fuzzball’s conversion rate was 63% higher in the year after launch.

hero.alt: Fuzzball’s quiz progress bar: a line-drawn cat chases a ball of wool along the bar, then confetti goes off at the end

blocks.html:
A Shopify product quiz asks shoppers a few questions and recommends the right product or plan from their answers. Good quiz design makes every step feel like one quick decision.

Fuzzball sells cat food through a Shopify subscription, and its quiz is where every new plan starts. Customers were dropping off inside it, so it was the first thing I redesigned as part of the Shopify conversion rate optimisation work.

blocks.text: The problem with Fuzzball’s old quiz

blocks.html:
The problems with Fuzzball’s old quiz came out of my Shopify UX review. I went through every screen of the journey in Miro and pinned a note to everything that slowed customers down.

The quiz was hard work. Some screens mixed text inputs, radio buttons and tick boxes on the same step, so customers had to work out how to answer before they could answer. A selected answer looked the same as the Next button, so it wasn’t clear what you’d picked. A unit label looked like a button but wasn’t one. The Next and Back buttons moved to a different place on almost every screen.

There were also a lot of steps, with the most questions on the very first page. Some, like the cat’s birth month, didn’t change the plan at all.

blocks.alt: The Fuzzball UX review in Miro, with colour-coded notes across the quiz and the rest of the purchase journey
blocks.caption: The Fuzzball UX review in Miro. The quiz findings shaped the redesign.

blocks.html: The quiz wasn’t the only drop-off point. The bag was the other, because it wasn’t clear which items were the trial and which would repeat. The brief was to simplify both, show value at each step and keep the brand’s playful character.

blocks.text: The quiz starts before the quiz

blocks.html:
The Fuzzball quiz journey starts in the menu, not on the first question. The review found the buttons into the quiz said different things in different places, so customers couldn’t tell they all led to the same place. Now they all say Build Your Box.

The mobile and desktop menus carry a short how it works, plus quality and delivery messages, so customers trust the subscription before they start. The quiz header keeps How it works one tap away.

Product pages link straight into building a box, including for products you can only get through the quiz. On collection pages, subscription-only product cards show a lock and a View Product button instead of Add to Bag, so nobody finds out at checkout. I wrote about that card in more detail in Shopify product card design.

blocks.text: 1. One type of input per screen

blocks.html:
The first fix was consistency. Each screen of Fuzzball’s quiz now asks one question with one type of answer. The cat’s name is a single text field. What your cat eats and how much are big tappable cards with a product photo, one tap per answer.

Selected answers get a blue border and a tick, so they never look like the Next button. Next and Skip Questions sit in a fixed bar at the bottom of every step, in the same place every time. Next stays pale until you’ve answered, so you always know what the screen is waiting for. The recommended portion carries a label, and extra detail sits in slide-up panels instead of crowding the screen.

Clean, consistent and accessible screens are the point of Shopify UX and UI design: they let someone get through the quiz one-handed on a phone without thinking about the form.

blocks.alt: Three steps of Fuzzball’s Shopify quiz on mobile: the cat’s name, what type of food the cat eats, and how many cans a day, with the recommended portion labelled

blocks.text: 2. Fewer steps, agreed with the client

blocks.html:
Fuzzball’s quiz had more steps than it needed. I went through every question with the client and asked what each one was for. If an answer didn’t change the plan, it didn’t need to be a step.

The quiz now asks for your cat’s name, then what and how much your cat eats. The name carries through, so the next question asks what Luna eats, not what your cat eats. You can add another cat on the same screen instead of starting again.

Skipping was the client’s idea and mine together. Skip Questions sits on every step and takes you straight to a set meal plan, for anyone who already knows what they want or doesn’t want to answer questions at all.

blocks.text: 3. Giving the quiz its character back

blocks.html:
Stripping Fuzzball’s quiz back created a new problem. The review had called out the old quiz’s illustrations as one of its best bits, because they gave it so much personality. Once the quiz was clean, consistent and accessible, a lot of that character had gone. It worked, but it could have been any brand’s quiz.

The answer was already in the brand. Fuzzball uses hand-drawn illustrations, so I turned one of them into a progress bar with character. A line-drawn cat chases a ball of wool along the bar, and every step you complete moves it closer. Finish the quiz and the confetti goes off. The progress bar is something every quiz needs anyway. Making it the cat added character without adding a single step or getting in anyone’s way. It’s one of the microinteractions in Shopify design that does two jobs at once.

blocks.alt: Fuzzball’s quiz on mobile: answering each step moves the line-drawn cat along the progress bar after the ball of wool

blocks.html:
The rest of the character is in the details. Each step has its own background colour from Fuzzball’s palette, and the reviews sit at the top of every step, so the trust is there right through.

This is the bit I enjoy most about Shopify design: taking something functional and making it unmistakably the client’s brand.

blocks.text: 4. Making the end of the quiz honest

blocks.html:
The end of Fuzzball’s quiz is the bag, and it was the biggest drop-off point. The review found the shopping list was a long scroll down the page, and the bag asked again for choices customers had already made in the quiz.

The bag now separates the trial from the repeating order, so customers see exactly what they’re signing up to before they pay. Nobody subscribes by accident.

blocks.alt: Fuzzball’s bag on mobile, with tabs for today’s trial and the monthly plan, so the trial and the repeating order are shown separately

blocks.html: Checkout completion rose from 59% in the six months before launch to 82% in the five months after. Both figures cover the whole redesign, not the quiz alone. The quiz and the bag were the two places customers were leaving, and both were rebuilt as part of a bespoke Shopify store build. The full project is in the Fuzzball Shopify case study.

blocks.text: What to take for your own Shopify quiz

blocks.html:
• Review the quiz you have first. Go through every screen on a real phone and note everything that slows you down.
  • Use one input type per screen. Mixed fields make customers think about the form instead of their answer.
  • Keep the buttons in one place. Next and Back should never move between steps.
  • Question every step. If an answer doesn’t change the recommendation, cut the question.
  • Let people skip. Some customers already know what they want. A set plan gets them there faster.
  • Put the brand in the parts you need anyway. A progress bar, a button state or a loading screen can carry character without slowing anyone down.
  • Be clear about what repeats. Customers should know what they’re committing to before checkout.

faqs.q: What is a Shopify product quiz?
faqs.html: A Shopify product quiz is a short set of questions that recommends a product, bundle or subscription plan based on the shopper’s answers. It’s common in pet food, skincare and supplements, where customers aren’t sure what to buy.

faqs.q: How many steps should a Shopify quiz have?
faqs.html: A Shopify quiz should have as few steps as it takes to make a good recommendation. Every question should change the result. If it doesn’t, it’s slowing customers down for nothing.

faqs.q: Should customers be able to skip a Shopify quiz?
faqs.html: Yes. Some customers already know what they want, and making them answer questions can lose the sale. On Fuzzball, Skip Questions sits on every step and goes straight to a set meal plan, so the quiz helps people who want help without blocking anyone who doesn’t.

faqs.q: How do you keep a simple quiz on-brand?
faqs.html: Keep the questions plain and put the brand into the parts every quiz already has. On Fuzzball, the progress bar became an illustrated cat chasing a ball of wool, so the quiz stayed simple but still felt like Fuzzball.
